base.question: You have been given a pointy-topped regular hexagonal tile map consisting of 2 rows, where the first row has one tile and the second row has two tiles. Starting from a vertex, you will move along the edges of these tiles. Initially, you are positioned at the bottom right corner of the map, where you find a paddle wheel. You move up by one step, where you find a Gila monster. You move up-left by one step, where you find an African bush elephant. You move up by one step, where you find a flagpole. You move up-left by one step, where you find a barber chair. You move down-left by one step, where you find a trilobite. You move down by one step, where you find a wolf spider. You move down-right by one step, where you find a tiger cat. You move up-right by one step. What will you find? Your final answer must be only the object name (e.g., laptop). If you have not previously seen the object at the vertex, your final answer must be "unknown".

note: BBEH spatial reasoning, example 8.

base.question: Five allotment gardens lie side by side in a row, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right as seen from the path in front of them. Each garden belongs to a different person (Anton, Berta, Carl, Dora, Emil), grows mainly one vegetable (beans, carrots, leeks, onions, pumpkins) and has a shed of a different colour (brown, grey, black, orange, purple). The following is known: (1) The garden with the beans is directly to the left of the garden with the black shed. (2) Exactly one garden lies between the garden with the pumpkins and Anton's garden. (3) The garden with the grey shed is not Anton's garden. (4) The garden with the purple shed is directly next to the garden with the carrots. (5) Exactly one garden lies between the garden with the grey shed and the garden with the purple shed. (6) The garden with the brown shed is directly next to Carl's garden. (7) The garden with the leeks is somewhere to the left of Dora's garden, but not directly next to it. (8) The garden with the brown shed is not Dora's garden. (9) The garden with the orange shed is directly to the left of the garden with the leeks. (10) The garden with the carrots is directly next to Emil's garden. (11) The garden with the onions is Emil's garden. Which vegetable grows in the garden with the purple shed? Answer with one word.
base.note: Solution (position: owner, item, colour): 1: Carl, pumpkins, orange; 2: Berta, leeks, brown; 3: Anton, beans, purple; 4: Dora, carrots, black; 5: Emil, onions, grey. Why unique: exhaustive search over all 1,728,000 assignments leaves exactly this one, and no single clue states the asked pair. Tempting wrong answer: none in particular; any value that is consistent with a few clues only. Why a strong model may fail (untested): nothing is narrated, there is no sequence to follow; the clues must be combined by case analysis with backtracking.

base.question: Six people sit at a round table on six evenly spaced chairs, all facing the centre of the table. 'To the right of X' always means on X's own right-hand side. (1) Clara sits directly to the left of David. (2) Clara is the second person to the right of Felix. (3) Bruno and David do not sit next to each other. (4) Felix sits directly to the right of Ada. Who sits directly to the left of Eva? Answer with one name.
base.note: Solution: clockwise seen from above the order is Ada, Eva, David, Clara, Bruno, Felix. Facing the centre, a person's left-hand neighbour is the next one clockwise. Why unique: all 120 seatings (up to rotation) were checked; exactly one satisfies the clues, and the asked neighbour is not stated directly. Tempting wrong answer: Ada (the neighbour on the other side). Why a strong model may fail (untested): constraint solving on a circle where left and right are relative to each person.

base.question: Six children sit on a small round playground carousel, evenly spaced, with their backs to the centre: each of them faces outwards. 'To the right of X' always means on X's own right-hand side. (1) Rosa sits directly to the left of Pit. (2) Going clockwise as seen from above, Olga is the second person after Mona. (3) Sven is the second person to the right of Nils. (4) Olga and Rosa do not sit next to each other. Who sits directly to the left of Rosa? Answer with one name.
base.note: Solution: clockwise seen from above the order is Mona, Nils, Olga, Sven, Rosa, Pit. Facing OUTWARDS, a person's left-hand neighbour is the next one counterclockwise (the opposite of people facing the centre of a table). Why unique: all 120 seatings were checked. Tempting wrong answer: Pit (using the usual round-table rule for people facing inwards). Why a strong model may fail (untested): in tier 5 both test models failed circles facing outwards; here that frame is combined with constraint solving.

base.question: In a storeroom there are exactly three places where crates can stand, called place 1, place 2 and place 3. Five equally sized crates A, B, C, D and E are stacked as follows: on place 1, crate B stands on the floor with D on top of it; on place 2, crate A stands on the floor with C on top of it; on place 3, crate E stands alone. One move consists of lifting the topmost crate of one place and putting it down on another place (on the floor if that place is empty, otherwise on top of the stack there). The crates are to end up in one single stack on place 3, in alphabetical order with A on the floor and E on top. What is the smallest number of moves needed? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution (stacks bottom to top, places 1|2|3): BD|AC|E -> BDC|A|E -> BDCA|-|E -> BDCA|E|- -> BDC|E|A -> BD|EC|A -> B|ECD|A -> -|ECD|AB -> D|EC|AB -> D|E|ABC -> -|E|ABCD -> -|-|ABCDE. Why unique: breadth-first search over all configurations. Tempting wrong answer: 9 or 10 (forgetting that E must first leave place 3 and that A is buried under C), or the length of a longer working plan. Why a strong model may fail (untested): a plan must be optimised, not just found; temporary parking places are scarce.

base.question: Five colleagues need a meeting of exactly 50 minutes on Thursday. The office is open from 8:00 to 17:00; the meeting must lie completely within these hours and can start at any full five minutes. Their fixed appointments that day: Ahmed is at the dentist until 9:15, has a call from 10:30 to 11:20 and a workshop from 15:25 to 16:00. Birte teaches from 9:00 to 10:00, has lunch with a client from 12:00 to 12:45 and leaves for good at 16:30. Chen arrives at 8:30, is in the lab from 11:00 to 12:10 and has a review from 13:30 to 14:15. Dana has a call from 10:40 to 11:10, is out from 12:30 to 13:40 and leaves for good at 16:00. Emre is on a train until 9:30, has a short call from 13:00 to 13:20 and an interview from 15:10 to 15:40. Outside these times everybody is available. A meeting may begin at the minute an appointment ends and end at the minute one begins. Suppose it is enough if Birte and at least three of the other four take part for the whole 50 minutes. What is the earliest time at which such a meeting can start? Answer as H:MM.
base.note: Solution: at 13:40 the following are free for the full 50 minutes: Ahmed, Birte, Dana, Emre. No earlier five-minute start has Birte and three others free throughout. (With all five the earliest start would be 14:15.) Why unique: every start time was checked. Tempting wrong answer: 14:15 (the answer for all five) or 8:30 (Birte is free only until 9:00). Why a strong model may fail (untested): a quorum with one fixed member; every candidate time needs a count over five calendars.

base.question: Mia and Tom renovate a room together on a Saturday. The jobs: strip the old wallpaper (3 hours); fill the cracks (2 hours, only after the wallpaper is off); let the filler dry (2 hours, nobody has to be there); paint the ceiling (2 hours, only after the filler is dry); paint the walls (3 hours, only after the ceiling is painted); hang the lamp (1 hour, only after the ceiling is painted); carry the old sofa down to the street (1 hour, needs both of them at the same time, possible at any time); assemble the new shelves in the hall (6 hours, possible at any time); clean the windows (3 hours, possible at any time); varnish the door (3 hours, possible at any time). Unless stated otherwise a job needs exactly one person, and two people cannot speed it up. A job, once begun, is finished without interruption by the same person. Both work equally fast and take no breaks. What is the smallest number of hours after which all jobs can be finished? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution: two lower bounds both fall short. The chain wallpaper 3 + filler 2 + drying 2 + ceiling 2 + walls 3 needs 12 hours; the total work is 25 person-hours, i.e. at least 12.5 hours for two people. The true minimum is 13 hours. One possible plan (start hours): strip the old wallpaper 0, assemble the new shelves in the hall 0, fill the cracks 3, let the filler dry 5, carry the old sofa down to the street 6, paint the ceiling 7, clean the windows 7, paint the walls 9, varnish the door 10, hang the lamp 12. Why unique: exhaustive schedule generation over all job orders (with unlimited helpers it would be 12 hours). Tempting wrong answer: 12 (the longest chain) or 12.5 (work divided by two). Why a strong model may fail (untested): neither simple bound is attainable, because jobs cannot be split and the sofa needs both people at once; an actual timetable must be constructed.

base.question: A camping grill has room for exactly four burgers at a time. Each burger must be grilled for 3 minutes on each of its two sides; a side must get its 3 minutes in one go, but the two sides need not be grilled directly one after the other, and a half-done burger may wait on a plate. Turning burgers and swapping them takes no time. What is the smallest number of minutes in which five burgers can be completely grilled? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution: ten sides, four per round, need at least three rounds, and three are enough: round 1 burgers 1-4 (first side); round 2 burgers 1-3 (second side) and burger 5 (first side); round 3 burgers 4 and 5 (second side). 3 x 3 = 9 minutes. Why unique: brute force over all round assignments. Tempting wrong answer: 12 (four burgers on both sides, then the fifth on both sides). Why a strong model may fail (untested): the batch-wise habit hides the interleaved plan; it is the known three-pancake idea with numbers for which no memorised answer exists.

base.question: In a certain year the 1st of March is a Friday. How many Fridays does the month of May have in that year? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution: March has 31 days, so 1 April is a Monday; April has 30 days, so 1 May is a Wednesday. The Fridays in May are the 3, 10, 17, 24, 31: 5. Why unique: calendar arithmetic (checked with 2024). Tempting wrong answer: 4. Why a strong model may fail (untested): two month lengths and the fact that a 31-day month has five of three weekdays.

base.question: Lea has 2 sisters and 1 brother. Her mother has exactly one sister and two brothers. The mother's sister has no children; she has 5 nephews and 6 nieces in total. Lea's father has exactly one brother and two sisters. This brother has 4 nephews and 5 nieces in total and, in addition, 3 daughters of his own and no sons. In this family, 'nephews' and 'nieces' are only the children of a person's own brothers and sisters, and 'cousins' are only the children of the brothers and sisters of one's parents. There are no half-siblings, and nobody has children with a relative. How many cousins does Lea's brother have? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution: Lea's parents have 4 children (1 son, 3 daughters). The childless aunt's 11 nephews and nieces include these 4, so the mother's brothers have 7 children. The father's brother's 9 nephews and nieces also include Lea's 4 siblings-and-self, leaving 5 children of the father's sisters; his own 3 daughters are cousins too. Total 15. Why unique: computed from an explicit family tree. Tempting wrong answer: 23 (nothing subtracted), 19 (subtracted only once) or 12 (uncle's daughters forgotten). Why a strong model may fail (untested): the asked person's own family is hidden twice inside the given totals (the pattern of the hard 'Alice in Wonderland' questions, with new numbers and structure).

base.question: The footpaths of a large park form a honeycomb pattern: regular hexagons, all of the same size, fitted together without gaps. Two sides of every hexagon run exactly north-south; the other sides run diagonally, either north-east/south-west or north-west/south-east. Three paths meet at every junction. Noah walks from junction to junction; each stage of the walk follows exactly one side of a hexagon from one junction to the next. He starts at a junction with a drinking fountain and walks thirteen stages in these directions: north-east, south-east, north-east, south-east, south, south-west, north-west, south-west, south, south-west, north-west, north, north-west. Now he wants to return to the drinking fountain along the paths by the shortest possible way. How many stages does this shortest way back have? Answer with a number.
base.note: Solution: after thirteen stages he is only 3 path sides away from the start (breadth-first search on the honeycomb). Why unique: computed by script. Tempting wrong answer: 13 (walking back the same way) or 1. Why a strong model may fail (untested): the end position must be located on the honeycomb and a shortest path found; nothing in the text says how far he has come.
